'''Donald Erik Sarason''' (January 26, 1933 – April 8, 2017) was an American [[mathematician]] whose research topics included [[Hardy space]] theory and [[Vanishing mean oscillation|VMO]]. As a professor at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] he became the [[doctoral advisor]] of 39 graduate students.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/eastbaytimes/obituary.aspx?n=donald-e-sarason&pid=185050514&fhid=5486|title=Donald E. Sarason's Obituary on East Bay Times|work=legacy.com|accessdate=29 April 2017}}</ref>

==Education==
Sarason majored in physics at the [[University of Michigan]], graduating in 1955. After continuing for a master's degree in physics in 1957, he switched to mathematics, still at the University, completing his Ph.D. in 1963 under the supervision of [[Paul Halmos]].<ref>{{mathgenealogy|5021}}</ref>

==Career==
Sarason became a postdoctoral research at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in 1963–1964, supported by a [[National Science Foundation]] Postdoctoral Fellowship.
He joined the [[University of California Berkeley]] as an assistant professor in 1964, was tenured as an associate professor in 1967, and promoted to full professor in 1970. He retired in 2012.

==Selected works==
*1967. Generalized Interpolation in <math>H^\infty</math>.<ref name="gen-interp">Sarason, D. Generalized Interpolation in <math>H^\infty</math>. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 127:179–203, 1967.</ref><br/>Sarason reproved a theorem of G. Pick<ref>Pick, G. Über die Beschränkungen analytischer Funktionen, welche durch vorgegebene Funktionswerte bewirkt werden. Math. Ann., 77:7–23, 1916.</ref> on when an interpolation problem can be solved by a holomorphic function that maps the disk to itself; this is often called [[Nevanlinna-Pick interpolation]]. Sarason’s approach not only gave a natural unification of the Pick interpolation problem with the Carathoédory interpolation problem (where the values of <math>\phi</math> and its first <math>N-1</math> derivatives at the origin are given), but it led to the Commutant Lifting theorem of Sz.-Nagy and Foiaş<ref>Szokefalvi-Nagy, B. and Foiaş, C. Commutants de certains opérateurs. Acta Sci. Math. (Szeged), 29:1–17, 1968.</ref> which inaugurated an operator theoretic approach to many problems in function theory.
*1975. Functions of Vanishing Mean Oscillation.<br/> Sarason’s work played a major role in the modern development of function theory on the unit circle in the complex plane. In Sarason<ref name="gen-interp"/> he showed that <math>H^\infty + C</math> is a closed subalgebra of <math>L^\infty</math>. Sarason’s paper<ref>Sarason, D. Algebras of Functions on the Unit Circle. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc., 79:286–299, 1973.</ref> called attention to outstanding open questions concerning algebras of functions on the unit circle. Then in a 1975 paper,<ref>Sarason, D. Functions of Vanishing Mean Oscillation. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 207:391–405, 1975.</ref> Sarason introduced the space VMO of functions of vanishing mean oscillation. A complex-valued function defined on the unit circle in the complex plane has vanishing mean oscillation if the average amount of the absolute value of its difference from its average over an interval has limit <math>0</math> as the length of the interval shrinks to <math>0</math>. Thus VMO is a subspace of the set of functions with bounded mean oscillation, called [[Bounded mean oscillation|BMO]]. Sarason proved that the set of bounded functions in VMO equals the set of functions in <math>H^\infty + C</math> whose complex conjugates are in <math>H^\infty + C</math>. Extensions of these ideas led to a description of the closed subalgebras between <math>H^\infty</math> and <math>L^\infty</math> in Chang<ref>Chang, Sun Yung A. A Characterization of Douglas Subalgebras. Acta Math., 137:82–89, 1976.</ref> (written by one of Sarason’s former students) and Marshall.<ref>Marshall, Donald E.  Subalgebras of <math>L^\infty</math> containing <math>H^\infty</math>. Acta Math., 137:91–98, 1976.</ref>
*1978. Function Theory on the Unit Circle. Notes for lectures at a conference at [[Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University]], Blacksburg, Virginia, June 19–23, 1978.<br/> On June 19–23, 1978, Sarason gave a series of ten lectures at a conference hosted by Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (now Virginia Tech) on analytic function theory on the unit circle. In these lectures he discussed a number of recent results in the field, bringing together classical ideas and more recent ideas from functional analysis and from the extension of the theory of Hardy spaces to higher dimensions. The lecture notes, entitled Function Theory on the Unit Circle were made available by the math department at VPI.
*1994. Sub-Hardy Hilbert Spaces in the Unit Disk.<ref>Sarason, D. ''Sub-Hardy Hilbert spaces in the unit disk'', volume 10 of ''University of Arkansas Lecture Notes in the Mathematical Sciences''. John
Wiley & Sons, Inc., New York, 1994. A Wiley-Interscience Publication.
</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Review of ''Sub-Hardy Hilbert spaces in the unit disk'' by D. Sarason|author=Rovnyak, James|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|volume=33|year=1996|pages=81–85|doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-96-00634-9|doi-access=free}}</ref><br/> This book developed the theory of the  de Branges–Rovnyak spaces <math>\mathcal{H}(b)</math>, which were first introduced in de Branges and Rovnyak.<ref>de Branges, Louis and Rovnyak, James. ''Square summable power series''. Holt, Rinehart and Winston, New York-Toronto, Ont.-London, 1966.</ref> Sarason pioneered the abstract treatment of contractive containment and established a fruitful connection between the spaces <math>\mathcal{H}(b)</math> and the ranges of certain Toeplitz operators. Using reproducing kernel Hilbert space techniques, he gave elegant proofs of the Julia–Carathéodory and the Denjoy–Wolff theorems. Two recent accounts of the theory are Emmanuel Fricain and Javad Mashreghi<ref>Fricain, Emmanuel and Mashreghi, Javed. ''The theory of <math>\mathcal{H}(b)</math> spaces''. Vol. 1, volume 20 of ''New Mathematical Monographs''. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 2016.
</ref> and Dan Timotin.<ref>Timotin, Dan. A short introduction to de Branges–Rovnyak spaces. In
''Invariant subspaces of the shift operator'', volume 638 of ''Contemp. Math.'', pages 21–38. Amer. Math. Soc., Providence, RI, 2015.</ref>
*2007. Complex Function Theory: Second Edition. The [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>Sarason, Donald. ''Complex Function Theory'', second edition. American Mathematical Society, Providence, 2007.</ref><br/> This textbook for a first course in complex analysis at the advanced undergraduate level provides an introduction to the theory of analytic functions.
